item.title: Fall Foliage Hike — Thu Nov 12, 9:00 AM — Old Creedmoor Nature Preserve
item.description:

item.title: AI Assisted Programming for STEM — Thu Nov 12, 1:00 PM — The TEC - Technology Engagement Center
item.description:
This class introduces scientists and engineers to using AI tools to support quantitative programming tasks in Python. We'll focus on how AI can help with common STEM workflows such as data extraction and cleaning, basic modeling with tools like scikit-learn, interpreting results, and debugging code.
A major emphasis of the session is safe and responsible use. We'll discuss what AI is (and is not), why its outputs are nondeterministic, how it differs from primary sources like documentation and textbooks, and when you should verify or reject AI-generated suggestions. The class is designed for undergraduates, graduate students, or professionals with some programming experience who want to learn how to use AI to work more efficiently
Source: Duke University

item.title: Distingusihed Seminar Series w/ Dr. Jenny Amos — Thu Nov 12, 3:00 PM — Wilkinson 021
item.description:
Process Over Answers: Using Scaffolded Pedagogy to Combat Cognitive Offloading in the Age of AI
As Generative AI tools make final answers instant and effortless, engineering educators face a critical challenge: preventing students from bypassing the "productive struggle" necessary to build genuine critical thinking skills. When students rely on automated outputs or template-driven shortcuts, they risk developing an illusion of competence that fails under complex, open-ended problem-solving.
This seminar presents empirical insights and actionable strategies from a foundational sophomore course designed to transition students from "activists", who jump straight to calculations, into deliberate "reflectors", who focus on understanding the problem before attempting to solve. We found that incoming students enter with low reflective learning habits, but integrating explicit metacognitive instruction, structured problem-solving frameworks, and active group learning yielded dramatic growth

item.title: Why Did Confucius Say "I Don't Know"? — Thu Nov 12, 3:10 PM — Friedl 126
item.description: Humility in knowing is often associated with recognizing that one may be mistaken, acknowledging one's limitations, and restraining excessive confidence. But simply saying "I don't know" seems to go further. It may sound like an admission of ignorance, or even a surrender of one's standing as a knower. Puzzlingly, however, Confucius makes just such a declaration in Analects 9.8. This talk asks how his "I don't know" can still be understood as a form of humility in knowing. I develop an answer through Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming, two of the most influential Neo-Confucian philosophers. I argue that their thought allows us to reconstruct a form of humility that goes beyond familiar accounts centered on fallibility, cognitive limitations, and the regulation of confidence. What is lowered in this deeper form of humility is the authority of the knowing subject itself. I call this "non-sovereign humility": a lowering of the subject's claim to control, possess, and finalize what becomes known wit

item.title: “Picturing the Persianate Book: A Short Introduction” — Thu Nov 12, 4:00 PM — Smith Warehouse - Bay 10
item.description:
Persian illustrated manuscripts and album paintings from early modern times are replete with representations of books in myriad forms and contexts. This talk explores such metapictures and looks at how, where, when and why books are depicted and what such images have to tell us about manuscript materials, manuscript making and manuscript use in Iran and India during the 14th through early 17th centuries.
Marianna Shreve Simpson (Ph.D., Harvard) Has published, taught, and lectured widely on medieval and early modern Islamic art in general and the arts of the book in particular. Over the years she has taught at various American universities and institutions, including for the University of Virginia's Rare Book School. She is currently affiliated with the Schoenberg Institute of Manuscript Studies at the University of Pennsylvania.
The talk will take place in Room A266 Bay 10 on the second floor of Smith Warehouse.
Source: Duke University

item.title: The Inoperative Left, or, How to Philosophize with a Broken Hammer — Thu Nov 12, 4:30 PM — Friedl 225
item.description:
The Program in Literature presents
The Srinivas Aravamudan Annual Lecture in Critical Theory November 2026
Bruno Bosteels
Talk: The Inoperative Left, or, How to Philosophize with a Broken Hammer
Thursday, November 12, 2026 4:30pm - 6:00pm Friedl Buildling, Room 225
In this talk, Bruno Bosteels will trace a polemical genealogy of inoperativity as a keyword in what he describes as the jargon of finitude, with which contemporary post-Heideggerian philosophies seek to come to terms with the defeat of the Left.
Bruno Bosteels is Dean of Humanities and Jesse and George Siegel Professor in the Humanities in the Department of Latin American and Iberian Cultures, with a joint appointment in the Institute for Comparative Literature and Society, at Columbia University.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Qualitative Research Ethics Workshop — Thu Nov 12, 5:00 PM — None
item.description:
Thinking about conducting interviews or other qualitative research for your senior thesis? This workshop will help you turn your research question into a plan and start thinking through the practical steps involved in conducting research responsibly.
By the end of the workshop, you'll have the tools to:
~Translate your research question into a qualitative research design. ~Begin assessing potential risks associated with your proposed research. ~Get started on an IRB (Institutional Review Board) application for your project.
You'll also get access to resources to help you continue developing and refining your research design after the workshop.
Interested in interviewing people for your honors thesis but not sure where to start? Haven't thought much about research ethics or potential risks yet? This workshop is a great place to start!
Source: Duke University

This year's program will showcase highlights of the Forest's work across its three strategic areas-teaching and research, management and stewardship, and community engagement-demonstrating the enduring value of the Duke Forest as a living laboratory, an experiential classroom, a model for sustainable resource management, and a cherished community resource.

item.description:
November 12, 2026. Ahmadieh Family Lecture. Smith Warehouse, Bay 4. 6:00 pm SCREENING. SEEDS. (2025) 123". Britanny Shyne. Interweaving the stories of three Black generational farmers to create a collective and intimate portrait of farming today, Seeds is a moving and powerful exploration of their lives, joys, and struggles as well as the fragility of legacy and owning land. With remarkable intimacy, the film documents their everyday lives - cotton harvesting, chasing cows, dealing with broken machinery and financial precarities.

item.description:
Join us for a special conversation with Duke Sanford Dean JR DeShazo and Sanford Professor The Honorable John Hillen as they explore the role of civic participation, democratic leadership, and constructive engagement in strengthening our democratic institutions.
The Duke Sanford Development and Alumni Relations team invites Duke alumni, parents, and friends to an engaging discussion about how these principles shape Sanford's teaching and its commitment to preparing students for thoughtful, effective participation in public life. We look forward to an evening of thoughtful conversation and meaningful exchange.

item.title: Annual Eugene A. Stead Jr., MD, Medicine Grand Rounds: From Durham to Singapore and Back: The Global Impact of Duke-NUS Medical School — Fri Nov 13, 8:00 AM — Duke South Clinic - Amphitheater

Tom Coffman, MD, will present "From Durham to Singapore and Back: The Global Impact of Duke-NUS Medical School" as the keynote speaker for the Department of Medicine's Annual Eugene A. Stead Jr., MD, lecture held in conjunction with the School of Medicine's Medical Alumni Weekend.
Dr. Stead's leadership lead to the formation of the Duke Databank for Cardiovascular Diseases, which grew into the Duke Clinical Research Institute, and he helped make of a new profession when he created the role of physician assistant. Duke's PA program was the first in the country and is currently the top PA program in the nation. item.description: Liberty Arts is proud to announce the 10th Annual Iron Pour, taking place on November 14, 2026, from 4-9pm. Register to attend so we know you’ll be there! Every November since 2016, Liberty Arts has hosted a FREE public arts event in Durham Central Park. All evening and into the night, thousands of pounds of molten iron will be poured into molds in an exciting fiery display, creating iron tiles designed by the public and sculptures made by NC artists. The event will also feature performances, local food trucks, craft beer, art vendors, and opportunities to learn from and engage with this spectacular art form. The Iron Pour has become a major cultural anchor in Durham, bringing together thousands of people to celebrate fire, metal, and creative expression in a dynamic, interactive setting. item.title: Downtown Durham African American Historian-Guided Tour — Sat Nov 14, 4:00 PM — CCB Plaza
item.description:
Durham: the mecca of black capitalism and the center of North Carolina’s African American business community. Join a local historian on this guided walking tour of Durham’s Black Wall Street, hearing the stories of how a humble sharecropper became the owner of the largest black-ned company in American history, and seeing some of the sites related to their stories. Learn how businessmen, labor organizers, educated academics, and craftsmen each contributed to the unique history of Durham’s African American community.

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Tue Feb 9, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Wed Feb 10 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description: Abstract: Biological-aging measures summarize physiological functioning across bodily systems and offer a way to examine how social inequality becomes embodied. This talk synthesizes four studies using biomarker data from the Health and Retirement Study and National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. The studies document racial and ethnic differences in biological aging partly associated with childhood socioeconomic conditions and education; widening educational inequality despite overall population improvements; economic, social, psychological, and behavioral pathways linking education to biological aging; and racial, ethnic, and nativity differences in the predictors and health consequences of accelerated aging. PineCone’s Old Time Jam takes place on the 2nd Thursday of each month from 7-9 p.m. at Riparian Provision Company (1408 South Saunders Street, Raleigh). This is an up-to-speed, gather-in-a-circle kind of jam. It’s led by great players who work to make sure there’s space for everyone in the tunes.
The leader picks a key (D, A and G are popular) and calls tunes in that key until it feels right to pick a new key and retune. The fiddlers traditionally call the tunes, but they’re not always the jam leader. If you’re playing fiddle you should expect to be asked, “Hey, you got a good D tune?” While “no” is an acceptable answer, it’s good to have a tune in each key that you’d feel comfortable calling and kicking off.

item.title: Canceled: The History Lake James: From Native Lands to Modern Recreation — Sat Nov 14 — Lake James State Park
item.description:
Join us at Lake James State Park for “The History of Lake James: From Native Lands to Modern Recreation.” This program explores the rich cultural and historical timeline of the settlement and development of Lake James, from the Indigenous tribes who first lived along the banks of the rivers, to the development of hydroelectric generation that created the lake as we know it, and finally to today’s recreational opportunities within the state park and surrounding area. It’s a great way to learn how the landscape and its uses have transformed over time while enjoying the natural beauty of Lake James.
Source: NC Cultural Resources
